question: What is the main goal of cancer rehabilitation?
explanation: You got this! Cancer rehab is all about helping patients get back their strength, independence, and good quality of life after treatment. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h1)

question: When should the cancer rehabilitation process ideally start?

options.A: Only after chemotherapy is fully completed
options.B: At the time of cancer diagnosis
options.D: When the patient enters palliative care

explanation: Starting early is key! When we begin rehab right from diagnosis, we can stop long-term physical problems before they even start. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h1)

question: What do we call a rehab goal that tries to stop side effects before they even happen?
explanation: Think of this as stopping trouble before it starts. Preventative rehab jumps in early to block expected physical losses. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h2)

question: A patient with advanced, progressive cancer is admitted for rehab. Which goal makes the most sense?
explanation: When the disease is advanced, our main priority shifts to keeping the patient comfortable, peaceful, and full of dignity. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h2)

question: Which health worker helps patients learn how to dress, cook, and do daily chores again?
explanation: Great job! Occupational therapists (OTs) focus on everyday life skills and help patients master their daily self-care tasks independently. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h3)

question: Why do we need a whole team of different specialists for cancer rehab?

options.A: The physical and emotional needs of survivors are too diverse for one discipline
options.B: It lowers the overall cost of hospital administration
options.C: Hospital rules require multiple signatures for every session
options.D: Doctors are no longer involved in direct patient care

explanation: Cancer touches every part of a person's life, so it takes a collaborative team of different experts to provide truly great care. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h3)

question: As a nurse, what common myth about weakness in cancer patients should you avoid?

options.A: Thinking it has no relationship to chemotherapy
options.B: Assuming it is simply due to aging or lack of effort
options.C: Believing it can only be cured by heavy weightlifting
options.D: Stating that it always resolves immediately after surgery

explanation: Never assume a weak patient is just being lazy or getting old! Cancer weakness comes from the disease, poor nutrition, and heavy treatments. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h4)

question: Why do nurses need to check and re-check a patient's physical abilities regularly during cancer care?

options.A: Therapists need to change their billing codes frequently
options.B: Initial assessments are usually inaccurate due to stress
options.C: Hospital accreditation requires weekly paperwork updates
options.D: A patient's functional status can fluctuate rapidly during treatment

explanation: Because treatments and cancer can change a patient's strength quickly up or down, regular check-ins help us keep our care plan on track. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h4)

question: How is cancer-related fatigue different from everyday tiredness?

options.A: It does not improve with regular rest or sleep
options.B: It exclusively affects older adult populations
options.C: It only occurs during the first week of diagnosis
options.D: It can only be treated with high-dose intravenous vitamins

explanation: Cancer fatigue is heavy and overwhelming. Unlike normal tiredness, sleeping or resting doesn't make it go away. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h5)

question: Why is getting pain under control so important before starting rehab exercises?

options.A: Therapy sessions are legally required to be painless
options.B: Uncontrolled pain prevents patients from participating in therapy
options.C: Pain medication replaces the need for any physical movement
options.D: Physical therapists are not allowed to touch patients who have pain

explanation: It makes total sense: if a patient is hurting badly, they won't want to move, and they won't be able to do their recovery exercises. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h5)

question: When planning exercises for a patient whose cancer has spread to the bones, what must you guard against?
explanation: Bones weakened by cancer metastases are very fragile. We must avoid high-impact movements to prevent unexpected bone breaks. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h6)

question: A cancer patient is exercising. Which sign means you should stop the activity right away?

options.A: A slight increase in heart rate during active movement
options.B: Mild muscle soreness in the legs after walking twenty steps
options.C: Sudden chest pain, severe shortness of breath, and dizziness
options.D: Desire to rest after completing a supervised stretching routine

explanation: Always watch out for red flags! Chest pain, dizziness, and trouble breathing mean the heart or lungs are struggling during exercise. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h6)

question: Why is poor nutrition (malnutrition) such a big problem during cancer treatment?

options.A: It causes immediate and permanent hair loss
options.B: It increases the likelihood of bone fractures
options.C: It prevents medications from dissolving in the stomach
options.D: It impairs wound healing and reduces treatment tolerance

explanation: Good food is body fuel! Without proper nutrition, the body struggles to heal wounds and handle harsh cancer treatments. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h7)

question: What is the best eating strategy for a patient dealing with severe nausea and poor appetite?

options.A: Encouraging three large, heavy meals to catch up on lost calories
options.B: Forcing the patient to finish everything on a large dinner plate
options.C: Withholding all food until appetite returns spontaneously
options.D: Serving small, frequent nutrient-dense meals throughout the day

explanation: Huge meals can make a nauseous patient feel worse. Small, tasty bites spaced through the day are much easier to manage! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h7)

question: Besides the patient, who else is at high risk and needs emotional support during cancer recovery?
explanation: Don't forget the family! Caregivers pour so much energy into helping others that they often face severe stress and burnout themselves. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h8)

question: How should a nurse respond when a patient expresses deep fear that their cancer will return?

options.A: Change the subject immediately to something more positive
options.B: Acknowledge their feelings and provide a safe space to talk
options.C: Assure them with certainty that the cancer will never come back
options.D: Tell them not to worry because worrying brings the cancer back

explanation: Empathy first! Validating their fears and being there to listen helps them process heavy emotions instead of bottling them up. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h8)

question: What is the main purpose of a survivorship care plan?

options.A: To manage acute surgical complications in the hospital
options.B: To replace the need for any further primary care visits
options.C: To guarantee that cancer will never return in the future
options.D: To outline treatment history and schedule ongoing surveillance

explanation: Think of it as a roadmap. A survivorship plan summarizes past treatments and maps out future health check-ups. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h9)

question: Which nursing activity is vital for long-term cancer survivors?

options.A: Administering initial chemotherapy cycles in the acute ward
options.B: Performing major reconstructive surgeries in the clinic
options.D: Monitoring for late-appearing side effects of treatment

explanation: Even years later, survivors can develop delayed side effects affecting their heart or lungs, making watchful nursing care essential. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T11#GNS321_U1_T11_h9)
